P1.evidence: The strongest setter read-back in the batch — 'I talked with Kim, who you spoke to a few days ago... you're doing construction, and you're wearing a harness all day. And you've already made some solid changes with diets, dropping 15 pounds... And you have some sciatica issue' — delivered as a summary the prospect confirmed point by point. No four-part frame was set. Agreement was sought only on the summary's accuracy, 'Okay, so I'm in the right ballpark', not on how the call would run. The open question never arrived in scripted form; the closest equivalent came 20 minutes in as 'what made this moment? Like, why are we on this call?'

P2.evidence: Genuinely thorough. Injuries were pursued properly to frequency, duration, functional impact and what relieves them — 'how many times did it actually... What in total?', 'Were you able to work at that time?' — and closed out with 'Any other injuries, stiffness, anything in your body?'. Work was covered including the harness weight and hours, and daily energy was asked explicitly and well: 'after like a 8 to 10 hour day, like what's the fatigue feel like? Is it more like physical, mental, or both?' Nutrition went deep enough to surface the naturopath and the psoriasis. Weaknesses: age was never asked, height and weight were volunteered, health conditions were never asked as a category so the psoriasis emerged only via a diet question, hereditary history was never touched, and sleep was discussed largely through the rep's own experience rather than asked about.

P3.evidence: The magic-wand question ran well — 'If you had a magic wand and you could solve all of this tomorrow, what disappears and what actually becomes possible for you' — and the blocked-activity question landed, surfacing hiking and mountain biking. The 60-65 projection was asked. But the phase never got past the prospect himself: 'who else does that impact' was never asked, no spouse or children were ever explored on a 50-minute call, and the deepest frame was supplied by the rep rather than extracted — 'We don't want to age in a way that somebody has to take care of you, right?' There was no reflect-back at all, so the real driver, protecting his ability to keep earning in a body-dependent trade, was never named and mirrored.

P4.evidence: Well run. Past attempts were surfaced in detail — the gym split routine, the six-month early-morning habit, the Toronto coach he did not proceed with — and the rep pushed for the breakdown rather than accepting the first answer: 'What happened? Where did you, where did you stop?' That produced the real root cause, the move and the 45-minute commute forcing a 4am start until 'I just kind of got tired, kind of got burned out.' P4e is partial because the rep named the gap instead of letting the prospect name it: 'it wasn't really sustainable, like, it wasn't designed around your life.' The information-isn't-the-problem question was never asked.

P5.evidence: The two-year question ran nearly verbatim — 'if nothing changes, and you would stay in your current way of doing... what that actually look like in two, three, five years from now?' — but drew a mild answer ('I think it would be much of the same') that was never pressed. The willing-to-settle, why-not and line-in-the-sand moves were all absent. The strongest consequence material arrived too late, after the price objection: 'Every day you're basically risking a serious back injury... So let me ask you this, how much that actually costs you?' The prospect conceded it immediately, which suggests that frame built before the price would have changed the call.

P6.evidence: Both questions were asked and the second was pressed hard, which was good work — 'are you the kind of guy that's actually going to show up and do the work?' followed by 'You think, or you are?' The problem is what the answers were. The belief answer was hedged, 'Yeah, possibly', and the commitment answer was explicitly conditional: 'it all depends, too, with financial costs, too', immediately followed by disclosure of a competing fitness coach. That is textbook hesitation and the script says return to Phase 5. Instead the rep moved into the pillar presentation and then price, and every subsequent objection was the one already signposted here.

P11.evidence: A close was attempted at three price points and no payment was collected at any of them. The call ended on the prospect's hard stop with an agreement to email information about the $200/month community. Steps 2 to 4 unreachable.

objection_plays.detail: The isolate ran twice and ran well — 'If the money weren't a factor, like, does the program itself make sense for you, where you're trying to get to?' and then the stronger 'imagine this is for free. Yeah, but it's not. But if that was for free, like, would you actually do it?', which got an unambiguous yes and correctly established this as a capacity rather than a value problem. Having diagnosed it as capacity, the play then went entirely unrun: no should-I-versus-how reframe, no permission question for a financial conversation, and none of the six financial-picture items — no cash on hand, no monthly surplus after bills, no credit card count, no available credit, no investments. The rep substituted a single question the script does not contain, 'what's your budget range that you were thinking?', and then priced down to that number twice. This is the inverse error to the Mike Chenard call, where the full picture ran and revealed $50,000 of available credit; here the same picture was never attempted.

The trigger was explicit and was the real objection — 'maybe this is not the time for, like, maybe once I get this venture up and running and making a little bit more money where I have that much more disposable income'. Not one move was run. No 'things never slow down', no 'when does it actually become the right time', no 'the longer you wait the harder this gets', which was unusually available here given a degenerating back condition and a physically punishing job. The rep responded with a downsell instead, which conceded the timing premise rather than challenging it.

Triggered mildly — 'I consider it, and it takes some time to look at those things' and a request for a written breakdown. No play ran and the requested breakdown was never provided on the call, only promised by email for a different product.

Script gap, third instance in this batch: a cheaper or free alternative that would plausibly work. The prospect named two — a fitness-coach friend in Toronto who had offered one-to-one work with a nutrition plan and weekly updates, and, decisively, 'For that type of money, I can get my brother-in-law to train. He's been working out all his life.' Neither was addressed. The rep had earlier pre-empted the PT comparison with a business-model argument about teaching to fish, but never returned to it when the concrete substitute was named at the decisive moment.

Script gap: price opacity upstream. The prospect arrived with no price expectation and said so directly — the setter 'was a bit vague' and the application page never showed a figure, so 'I followed the rabbit hole'. The rep handled the immediate request competently by deferring until value was confirmed, but there is no play for a prospect who is discovering a $6,000 price for the first time 38 minutes into a call, and this is a funnel design problem rather than a rep failure.

Script gap and the most consequential: no clinical stop exists. The prospect disclosed years of recurrent sciatica with episodes that prevent him standing straight and cost him work, plus psoriasis and active naturopathic and acupuncture care. The playbook offers no clearance question, no clinician-contact step and no pause path, so the rep instead promised the mobility protocol would address the sciatica 'so it doesn't appear again'. Same missing gate as the Jan Falesnik call.

notes: Strong front half, no close mechanics. The baseline and past-attempts work were among the best in the batch, and the energy and injury questioning were genuinely good. Three fixable things. First, the commitment answer was conditional on money and the rep presented anyway — that hesitation predicted the entire second half of the call. Second, having correctly diagnosed a capacity objection, he ran none of the open-wallet financial picture and instead asked the prospect to name a budget, which guarantees a discount rather than a deal. Third, the cost-of-injury frame he eventually used was the right one and was deployed after the price instead of before it; on a prospect whose income depends on his back, that frame belongs in Phase 5. Separately and above coaching: the clinical disclosure here needed a clearance gate the process does not have.
